articles.title: Malária: Anvisa autoriza teste em humanos de vacina 100% brasileira
articles.description: A Agência Nacional de Vigilância Sanitária (Anvisa) autorizou o início de testes em humanos da primeira vacina do mundo contra a malária causada pelo Plasmodium vivax , parasita responsável pela maioria dos casos da doença no país. O imunizante é feito com tecnologia 100% nacional. Em nota, o Ministério da Saúde detalhou que a dose, chamada Vivaxin, é fruto de pesquisas conduzidas pelo Centro de Tecnologia de Vacinas (CTVacinas) da Universidade Federal de Minas Gerais (UFMG). A tecnologia tem incentivo previsto de R$ 12 milhões da pasta para ensaios clínicos de fases I, II e III. Notícias relacionadas: Meningite: quatro cidades do Rio ofertam vacina a pessoas até 24 anos. José Sarney é internado em UTI após procedimento abdominal. Vírus respiratórios ainda estão em alta no país, alerta Fiocruz. De acordo com o ministério, o estudo clínico de fase I vai avaliar a segurança da vacina, possíveis reações à aplicação e a capacidade de estimular uma resposta imunológica em um total de 48 participantes sem infecção prévia, com idades entre 18 e 59 anos. O acompanhamento clínico será feito por 360 dias. “O avanço na pesquisa da tecnologia representa um marco e abre a possibilidade de uma nova forma de prevenção contra a doença que, em 2025, registrou 118.037 casos no território nacional”, avaliou a pasta no comunicado. As duas vacinas contra malária atualmente recomendadas por autoridades sanitárias foram desenvolvidas para outra espécie de parasita causador da doença, o Plasmodium falciparum , predominante na África, não contra o Plasmodium vivax , que predomina nas Américas e na Ásia. A doença A malária é uma doença infecciosa causada por um parasita do gênero Plasmodium , transmitido para humanos pela picada de fêmeas infectadas dos mosquitos Anopheles (mosquito-prego), mais abundantes nos horários crepusculares, ao entardecer e ao amanhecer. “Não é uma doença contagiosa, ou seja, uma pessoa doente não é capaz de transmitir malária diretamente a outra pessoa”, reforçou o ministério. Também conhecida como impaludismo, paludismo, febre palustre, febre intermitente, febre terçã benigna, febre terçã maligna, a malária recebe ainda nomes populares como maleita, sezão, tremedeira, batedeira ou febre. “Toda pessoa pode contrair a malária. Indivíduos que tiveram vários episódios de malária podem atingir um estado de imunidade parcial, apresentando poucos ou mesmo nenhum sintoma. Porém, uma imunidade esterilizante, que confere total proteção clínica, até hoje não foi observada”, destacou a pasta. O ministério alerta ainda que, caso não seja tratado adequadamente, o paciente com malária pode ser fonte de infecção por meses ou mesmo anos, de acordo com a espécie parasitária em questão . No Brasil, a maioria dos casos da doença se concentram na região amazônica, composta pelos seguintes estados: Acre, Amapá, Amazonas, Maranhão, Mato Grosso, Pará, Rondônia, Roraima e Tocantins. “Na região extra-amazônica, composta pelas demais unidades federativas, apesar das poucas notificações, a doença não pode ser negligenciada, pois a letalidade nesta região é maior que na região amazônica”, concluiu a pasta.

articles.description: Following the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, the federal government has formed an 11-member technocratic KP Advisory Council. The council will assist KP Governor Faisal Karim Kundi, who is now in charge of running the province, in exercising the functions of the KP government on behalf of the federal government. According to Information Minister Attaullah Tarar, the council comprises “competent” individuals as opposed to the PTI-led provincial government. Here is a breakdown of who is part of the council and what portfolio they have been assigned. Kifayatullah Khan Khan has been tasked with overseeing the provincial Home Department affairs. He previously served as the KP prisons inspector general (IG) and chairman of the Fata Tribunal. He is also the former secretary of the Home and Tribal Affairs Department and the ex-Mardan commissioner. Tariq Mehmood Pasha Tariq Mehmood Pasha, former chairperson of the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR), will be overseeing the province’s financial affairs. He was appointed as the FBR head in 2017 and has been described as a trusted aide of then-finance minister Ishaq Dar. He has also served at the Economic Affairs Division secretary and special assistant to the prime minister on finance. Amir Javed Supreme Court Advocate Amir Javed will be advising the KP governor on law. In 2023, he was appointed as the KP advocate general, at a time when he was serving as the additional attorney general for Pakistan. Earlier, he also served as the deputy attorney general. He resigned as the advocate general after the 2024 general elections. Syed Amir Abdullah Syed Amir Abdullah will be handling education-related matters in KP. He is a former caretaker provincial minister and an ex-member of the National Counter Terrorism Authority’s expert committee. He holds a PhD degree in international relations. Nigar Johar Khan Also included in the council is Lt Gen (retd) Nigar Johar Khan, whose life and career have been captured in a Pakistani film , ‘ Aik Hai Nigar ’. Lt Gen (retd) Johar is a graduate of the Army Medical College and holds an MCPS degree in family medicine, MSc in advanced medical administration and a Masters in Public Health. She has served as the National Instr­uctor of Hospital Prepar­edness in Emergency. Besides being the first female officer to be promoted to three-star rank, she was also the first female officer to command an army hospital, when she headed Combined Military Hospital, Jhelum, as a brigadier. At the time of her promotion, she was commanding the Military Hospital, Rawa­lpindi. She has been decorated with Tamgha-i- Imtiaz (Milit­ary) and is also the recipient of Fatima Jinnah Gold Medal for meritorious services in Army Medical Corps from the prime minister of Pakistan. Earlier this year, she also received the Hilal-i-Imtiaz. Sarfraz Ali Shah Sarfraz Ali Shah, who served as the adviser to the KP chief minister on planning and development from Aug 2024-Mar 2024, will be overseeing the matters of Mines and Minerals Department. He holds a PhD in economics. Muhammad Irshad Another FBR chairman has been included in the council, this time to oversee matters related to industries and commerce. Muhammad Irshad is also a member of the Pakistan Red Crescent Society’s management board and holds a PhD in finance. Asif Rafiq Ex-KP caretaker minister Asif Rafiq has been appointed to oversee the department of Communication and Works. Maulana Muhammad Tayyab Qureshi KP’s Chief Khateeb Maulana Muhammad Tayyab Qureshi will be advising the governor on religious affairs. He is the administrator of Jamia Ashrafia Peshawar and the prayer leader of Peshawar’s Mahabat Khan Mosque. articles.title: 'No lesson learnt': KP emergency evokes grim October memories
articles.description: Sunday, Oct 11, evoked grim memories for many in Pakistan, as the federal government imposed emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The cabinet was certain of the decision, but many others warned against repeating what they saw as an “ill-advised step”. Nevertheless, it happened, again. The threat of emergency and governor’s rule had been looming over the province for days, after the PTI announced its long march to Islamabad to demand the release of its jailed founder, Imran Khan. It materialised on Sunday. It began with a federal cabinet meeting where Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif was briefed on the security situation in KP, which the Centre had earlier been linking with the need for emergency in the province. The cabinet reviewed the situation, took note of the “provincial government’s deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism”, and gave the nod to impose emergency and governor’s rule in KP. A signature by President Asif Ali Zardari, and the decision was implemented shortly after. The development took veteran journalist Mazhar Abbas on a trip down memory lane, apparently a grim one. “Why [does] October often bring ‘bad news’ for democracy from 1958 to 2026?” he posted on X. “Saddest part is that each time one party or the other welcomed such moves. On Oct 12, 1999 when PM Nawaz was sacked, the PPP welcomed the move. Now, the PPP and PML-N agreed to get rid of the PTI KP government. No lesson learnt,” he lamented. Former ambassador and analyst Maleeha Lodhi agreed. “Really nothing learnt from history,” she too posted, replying to Abbas’s comment. Analyst Niaz Murtaza was more thorough in recounting the historical trend of what Abbas described as “bad news” from October. “October is perhaps the worst month for democracy,” Murtaza commented, sharing a list of instances from history: On the latest imposition of emergency in KP, he said the move was “deeply condemnable, unfortunate and ill-advised”. “The clearly illegitimate nature of the central government makes it doubly so. This could make the situation in KP much more complicated,” he warned. Others, too, warned against the move and its consequences. Among them was National Democratic Movement Chairperson Bushra Gohar, who posted a warning the night before emergency was imposed. “Emergency will further aggravate the already volatile political and security situation in Pakhtunkhwa. The province cannot afford yet another failed experiment after the disastrous pro-Taliban TTPTI government — 13 years of incompetence, loot and plunder, death and devastation,” she posted on X on the night before emergency was imposed. Instead, she added, free, fair and credible elections were the only way forward. Similarly, the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan cautioned the federal government and Parliament in a statement that declaring emergency or imposing governor’s rule in KP risked further deepening of political tensions and undermining of democratic processes. “We strongly urge the federal government and the PTI to resume a meaningful political dialogue immediately and ensure that citizens’ fundamental rights are not suspended under any pretext,” the statement said. Lawyer Rida Hosain said that by imposing emergency, the federal government has “undermined the democratic choice of the people of KP and its provincial autonomy”. “The authority of KP’s elected institutions flows from the people’s will, not from the dictates of the federal government,” she wrote on X. In another post, she pointed out that Article 175(3) of the Constitution had been deemed inapplicable for the duration of the emergency. “Article 175(3) mandates the separation of the judiciary from the executive. This paves the way for executive officers to perform judicial functions in these areas,” she explained. Similarly, journalist Munizae Jahangir termed emergency and governor’s rule a “spectacular failure of the politicians,the ruling party amd its allies”. They had set a “dangerous precedent and disenfranchised an entire province, while the opposition failed to negotiate a space for themselves where they could protect themselves and their citizens. The people of KP will now suffer the most,” she said. Lawyer Hassan Abdullah Niazi noted that throughout Pakistan’s history, the “imposition of an emergency has rarely resulted in better governance or democracy”. “We have normalised the extraordinary; the denial of fundamental rights,” he contended. He termed the decision “unconstitutional” and explained the reasons for his analysis in a series of posts on X. “Article 234 (governor’s rule) requires a demonstration that the constitutional machinery in a province has broken down. Nothing the government has said justifies this so far. The KP Assembly is working as is the cabinet,” Niazi explained. He went on to caution that “such a move will further fragment national stability” and “creates a dangerous precedent where the federation can simply dismiss troublesome provincial governments over political differences”. Senior journalist Zarrar Khuhro remarked, “While this has very little to do with terrorism, will emergency stop the bleeding. You guessed it: no.” Journalist Ihsanullah Tipu Mehsud saw emergency as a move that “frees the PTI” and “traps the Centre”. Because “Islamabad owns security, PTI owns the narrative”, he said on X. Former caretaker IT minister Umar Saif explained Mehsud’s deduction in more detail, saying that imposing emergency in KP “comes with an enormous burden of responsibility”. “It is not merely an exercise of authority; it is a commitment to fix what has gone wrong. The government must now deliver. Failure will deepen public disillusionment, hand fresh ammunition to the naysayers, and discredit the very idea of reform. “Reform demands clarity of intent, consistency of purpose, and the resolve to see it through. We have seen too many initiatives falter midway, leaving behind resentment and eroding faith in the process,” he said. Meanwhile, journalist Shahzad Iqbal noted that PPP Chairperson Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari had called emergency a “political atomic bomb”. “Yet President Zardari has completed hat-trick of imposing governor’s rule,” he said, recounting the previous two instances — in 2009 in Punjab and in 2013 in Balochistan. “The irony is hard to miss,” he commented. Pakistan’s former ambassador to the United States Husain Haqqani also noted the repeated instances of emergency and governor’s rule in Pakistan, commenting: “What has happened repeatedly in the brief history of Pakistan does not happen in the long history of other countries.” Header image: A general view shows a road blocked with shipping containers amid ongoing protests by the PTI party demanding the release of jailed former prime minister Imran Khan in Peshawar on October 11, 2026. — AFP

articles.title: FO reiterates Pakistan's 'firm and unshakeable' commitment to Saudi Arabia's security after Riyadh attack
articles.description: The Foreign Office (FO) on Sunday condemned a fresh wave of Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia, reaffirming Pakistan’s “firm and unshakeable” commitment to the sovereignty, territorial integrity, security and stability of the Gulf state under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement. The defence pact , of which Turkiye is also a part, was signed on August 7 and aims to strengthen collective deterrence and empower its signatory states to treat an attack against one of them as an attack against all of them. The statement comes following Saturday’s attack on Riyadh’s international airport, which killed at least 12 people and wounded 309 others. In a post on X, FO said the targeting of a civilian airport constituted “a heinous act of terrorism, a flagrant violation of international law and a grave threat to regional peace and security”. It expressed concern over the casualties resulting from the attack, extending condolences to the bereaved families and wishing a swift recovery to the injured. “The continued targeting of civilian population and critical infrastructure by the Houthi militia is utterly unacceptable and must be condemned unequivocally by the international community,” the statement read. It added: “Such brazen and indiscriminate acts of aggression cannot be justified under any circumstances and must cease immediately.” FO expressed “unwavering” solidarity with the leadership of Saudi Arabia and reiterated its “firm and unshakeable commitment” to Riyadh’s sovereignty, territorial integrity, security and stability in line with the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement and the “recent decision” taken by its Strategic, Political and Defence Committee on October 5, in which the member states had agreed to the rapid deployment of military forces and capabilities in the kingdom. The FO expressed support for Saudi Arabia’s right to self-defence against all threats and acts of aggression and went on to urge Yemen’s Houthis to cease attacks and the international community to take “a firm and unequivocal stand” against it. “Pakistan will continue to stand shoulder to shoulder with the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, resolute in its commitment to the kingdom’s sovereignty, security and defence.” Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, in a post on X, also condemned the attack. In his statement, the premier said that targeting civilian and critical infrastructure was “completely unacceptable and [constitutes] a serious threat to regional peace and stability. “Such acts of violence, which are a flagrant violation of international law, must cease immediately.” Expressing solidarity with Riyadh, PM Shehbaz said, “In accordance with the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement and the enduring bonds of brotherhood between our two countries, we reaffirm our steadfast commitment to Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and security.” Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar expressed concern at what he called the Houthi attack on the Riyadh airport. “We pray for the speedy recovery of all those injured, including the six Pakistani nationals,” he said. “Attacks targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure are totally unacceptable, violate international law and pose a serious threat to regional peace and security. Such acts must cease immediately,” he said. “We are in touch with the Saudi Authorities and are closely following the situation. I have directed our embassy in Riyadh to coordinate with the concerned authorities to provide all possible assistance to the injured Pakistani nationals,” he said. “We stand in solidarity with Saudi Arabia’s leadership and brotherly people. Pakistan remains firmly committed to the kingdom’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and security in accordance with the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement,” he said. PM Shehbaz also said that the embassy in Riyadh was in close contact with the Saudi authorities and was extending all possible assistance to the affected families. The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen has blamed the group for the strike on King Khalid International Airport, describing it as a “full-fledged war crime” that a diplomatic source attributed to a missile. Houthis have repeatedly targeted the facility, claiming a series of strikes on Thursday that killed three people and damaged a plane, though they did not announce any new attacks on Saturday. The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers after a truce in their long-running war with Yemen’s coalition government unravelled in July. Against this backdrop, Pakistan has repeatedly expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia. On Oct 5, in an emergency meeting of the Makkah pact in Riyadh, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkiye agreed to the rapid deployment of military forces and capabilities. Defence Minister Khawaja Asif, who was part of Pakistan’s delegation in the meeting, joined Geo News programme ‘Aaj Shahzeb Khanzada Kay Saath’ via telephone the same day and was asked about a possible operational role by Pakistan and Turkiye, to which he said both Turkiye and Pakistan had a “presence in theatre”, but only Saudi troops were involved in combat operations. On September 18, Inter-Services Public Relations Director General Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said Pakistan would go to “any extent” to defend the Gulf state, adding that Islamabad’s commitment to the kingdom’s security is “unconditional”. Asif has also reaffirmed that Pakistan will “practically and diplomatically” stand by Saudi Arabia against Yemen’s Houthi rebels if the situation escalates. The defence minister said that Pakistan would fulfil all its obligations under the Makkah Defence Alliance in accordance with the terms of the agreement between the three countries. At the same time, Pakistan has also asserted that the alliance is intended for collective deterrence and is defensive in nature.

articles.title: TSE atende Flávio e manda suspender canal do whatsapp Exército do Lula
articles.description: O presidente do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), ministro Kassio Nunes Marques, determinou neste domingo (11) a suspensão do canal “Exército do Lula”, criado no WhatsApp para postagens de apoio ao candidato à reeleição Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), que conta com cerca de 3,3 milhões de pessoas. O ministro atendeu ao pedido de suspensão protocolado pela campanha do candidato à Presidência da República Flávio Bolsonaro (PL). Notícias relacionadas: TSE manda Meta esclarecer restrições a postagens da campanha de Lula . TSE manda suspender site que oferece criptomoedas por apoio a Flávio. A campanha de Flávio alegou que o canal foi criado pelo deputado federal reeleito André Janones (Rede-MG) para disseminar desinformação sobre o cancelamento do Programa Bolsa Família, redução do valor de aposentadorias, entre outros casos. No entendimento de Kassio, o canal é responsável pela replicação de conteúdos que já foram considerados “inverídicos” pelo tribunal , como a afirmação de que Flávio seria favorável à retirada do título de Nossa Senhora Aparecida de padroeira do Brasil, além de afirmar que o candidato reduzirá aposentadorias se for eleito. “Quando essa mesma potência é posta a serviço da replicação de fatos que esta Corte já reconheceu como inverídicos, o dano ao equilíbrio do pleito é imediato e de difícil reversão”, afirmou. O presidente do TSE também afirmou que a "paridade de armas" deve ser garantida entre os candidatos. “A liberdade de expressão não é salvo-conduto para o ilícito eleitoral, e a paridade de armas entre os candidatos não sobrevive à conversão de uma ferramenta de comunicação em instrumento de desinformação em massa às vésperas do pleito”, completou. Competência Kassio ressaltou ainda que sua decisão foi tomada em função da proximidade do segundo turno das eleições. “O perigo na demora também está presente. O segundo turno das eleições realizar-se-á em 25 de outubro de 2026, e cada hora de funcionamento do canal amplia a exposição do eleitorado, com repercussão imediata e de difícil reversão”, justificou. A legalidade do canal “Exército do Lula” já estava judicializada no TSE antes da decisão do presidente da Corte. A campanha de Flávio ajuizou uma ação para cassar o mandato de Janones, além de solicitar a suspensão do canal. Neste sábado (10), o ministro Ricardo Vilas Bôas Cuêva, relator do processo, pediu que o presidenciável apresente informações complementares. Em suas redes, Janones rebateu a acusação de que utiliza o canal para disseminar notícias falsas. Segundo ele, o objetivo do canal é mobilizar e orientar eleitores durante o segundo turno das eleições presidenciais, que será disputado no dia 25, último domingo do mês, entre Flávio e Lula. Janones também enfatizou que não divulgou nenhuma notícia no canal. “A gente estava só mobilizando, crescendo páginas, trazendo pessoas, explicando como que iria funcionar”, complementou. Janones disse que o pedido da candidatura do PL é motivado por “medo”. “Eles pedem que eu seja proibido de criar outros canais. Sabe o nome disso? Medo. Eles estão com medo”, disse. *Colaborou Bruno de Freitas Moura, do Rio de Janeiro // Matéria ampliada às 13h28.

articles.title: Pakistan Army deployed in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa in aid of civil power
articles.description: ISLAMABAD: The federal government on Sunday authorised the deployment of Pakistan Army troops and assets in aid of civil power in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, after imposing an emergency and governor’s rule in the province. The authorisation of the army deployment was made through Statutory Regulatory Order, issued by the interior ministry on Sunday. According to the order, a copy of which is available with Dawn , the federal government authorised the deployment of army troops and assets in aid of civil power for the “safety of life, security of persons and property of citizens as well as security of government installations” in the province. The authorisation lasts for the duration of the proclamation issued regarding the imposition of an emergency and governor’s rule. The notification cited powers conferred to the government under Article 245 of the Constitution. KP Governor Faisal Karim Kundi, in consultation with the Military Operations Directorate at General Headquarters in Rawalpindi, would determine the number of troops and assets necessary, the notification added. Copies of the order were forwarded to the president’s secretary, prime minister’s adviser, the KP governor’s secretary, the Military Operations Directorate GHQ Rawalpindi, the KP home secretary, the inspector general of police (IGP) in the province, the Peshawar High Court registrar and other officials. The emergency imposition comes a day after PM Shehbaz met President Zardari and discussed the country’s overall security situation. That meeting came amid heightened tensions between the PML-N-led federal government and the KP government led by the PTI — which is in opposition in the Centre. They have been at odds over various issues, particularly on the counterterrorism policy, which was one of the main reasons behind the breakdown of their Oct 3 talks . Police guard a road leading to Red Zone, in Peshawar on October 11, 2026. — Reuters The PTI has said it was being left out of security decisions concerning KP, which the Centre has denied . It also calls for reviewing the counterterrorism policy and opposes military operations. On the other hand, the Centre has been criticising the KP government’s efforts to combat terrorism in the province and objects to its stance on dialogue with the Afghan Taliban. Shipping containers block roads Shipping containers were placed around the city of Peshawar to block roads after the imposition of the emergency. Containers were placed near Peshawar’s railway station to block the routes towards Khyber Bazaar, Shoba Bazaar and beyond. They were also placed near Edwardes College to block entry to Jail Road and Malik Saad Shaheed Flyover, while people were turned away from Sher Shah Suri Road as it was reported to be completely closed. Police were reportedly deployed in significant numbers, particularly around Governor House. The deployment included personnel called from other districts. Police and personnel of law enforcement agencies (LEAs), including many in plainclothes, were seen patrolling the roads leading to Governor House, the central police office, Peshawar police headquarters and other government installations largely located in the Red Zone, a correspondent reported. Vehicles with tinted glasses, police mobile vans, armored personnel carriers and other LEA vehicles were reportedly the only transport visible in and around the cantonment area, with life at a standstill and the area appearing deserted. Another correspondent reported that the road leading to Khyber Road was shuttered by a container and the traffic control gate closed. A large number of police personnel were also seen around Surey Pul, a favoured spot for protesters. Grand Trunk (GT) Road was blocked by containers at Firdous Chowk and the correspondent reported a large number of police personnel in the area. Only pedestrians were allowed to move ahead. Additionally, containers near Bala Hisar Fort and outside the Pakistan International Airlines (PIA) office on Arbab Road blocked entry towards Mall Road. A vehicle moves past a shipping container used to block a road leading to the Red Zone, in Peshawar on October 11, 2026. — Reuters Only official vehicles were being allowed to travel from Governor House towards the Chief Minister’s House, while tight security was reported on Sahibzada Abdul Qayyum road where they are located. The Civil Secretariat was seen to be deserted. Royal Artillery (RA) Bazaar has been closed, while Saddar remains partially open. Additionally, Peshawar’s Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) stations were reported to be shuttered by Dawn ’s correspondent. The stretch of Khyber Road connecting to University Road and Airport Road at Aman Chowk was reported to be open but with low traffic. A large police contingent was seen at Aman Chowk. Meanwhile, University Road was blocked by containers at Tehkal, and containers at Stadium Chowk allowed for only single-file passage of vehicles on both sides. Earlier, traffic jams were reported due to the closure of Khyber Road, which connects GT Road with the eastern side of University Road and serves as the main artery and choke point. The resulting diversions created pressure on auxiliary roads. The area is part of the cantonment, and the Red Zone contains important installations such as the Corps Commander’s House, civil secretariat, central police office, CM Secretariat, CM House and Governor House. All telecoms services, including landline and DSL, are reported to be suspended in the provincial capital. The city had witnessed a nearly 48-hour mobile service blackout just days ago, on account of the presence of the PTI in the city for its long march . With networks suspended, people faced immense issues in withdrawing money from bank accounts, as ATMs remained out of service for the entire day. Aside from the suspension of cellular network and broadband services, however, the situation remained normal for those living on Kohat Road, Charsadda Road, GT Road beyond Pir Zakorhi Bridge, and the area bordering the Khyber district, as well as others on the outskirts of the provincial capital. Vehicles of the armed forces were also reported to be patrolling cantonment areas and a heavy deployment of police was reported in both the city and its outskirts including Kohat Road, GT Road, University Road and Warsak Road. Separately, a holiday has been declared for schools, colleges and universities in the district on Monday (Oct 12), according to a notification issued by the deputy commissioner of Peshawar. “It is hereby notified that all educational institutions, both public and private, including schools, colleges and universities, shall remain closed on October 12, 2026 (Monday) located within the territorial jurisdiction of District Peshawar,” the notification said. On Saturday, KP Inspector General of Police (IGP) Zulfiqar Hameed put district police on alert for possible violent protests and sabotage in the event of an emergency in the province, emphasising caution in the use of force. Police personnel stand guard near shipping containers blocking a road leading to the Red Zone in Peshawar on October 11, 2026. — Reuters A notification issued by the IGP’s office directed not only officers in Peshawar but also district police officers (DPOs), sub-divisional police officers (SDPOs) and even station house officers (SHOs) to personally monitor the situation. It said DPOs could issue appropriate directions, instructions or guidelines to regulate protests and ensure public safety. In the event of violence, they could also take necessary legal action. It added that the use of force was to be carried out on a gradated basis, noting that in the first phase, protesters should be clearly warned against violence before police began to use forceful measures.

articles.title: Riyadh airport hit by fresh Houthi strike day after deadly attack
articles.description: A fresh Houthi strike hit Riyadh’s international airport on Sunday, a day after another attack claimed by the Yemeni group killed at least a dozen people and forced authorities to suspend operations at the facility. Saturday’s attack, the deadliest on Saudi soil in more than a decade, was a sharp escalation in the Yemen war , where Riyadh backs the internationally recognised government against the Houthis. The group on Sunday claimed multiple attacks over the last 24 hours, including on the airport, and threatened to keep targeting the kingdom’s transit hubs, calling them “a theatre of operations for our forces”. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group “carried out four qualitative operations in the past 24 hours using ballistic and cruise missiles and drones”. Saree said they targeted the Riyadh airport multiple times, as well as the Dammam airport and two facilities belonging to the Saudi state oil company Aramco. Hours later, the Saudi coalition fighting the group reported that a projectile struck King Khalid International Airport, sparking a fire. Air defences also intercepted a missile nearby, it added. The civil aviation authority said the attack caused an unspecified number of injuries, and that a damage assessment was underway. AFP journalists and locals reported hearing the sound of multiple blasts in the Saudi capital on Sunday. “The birds went into a frenzy after the sound. The whole house shook,” said one resident of the Al-Aarid neighbourhood in the north of the city. ‘Full-fledged war crime’ The Houthis have stepped up their attacks on the Riyadh airport — where three people were also killed on Thursday — as well as on other key targets in the world’s top crude oil exporter. And although Saudi Arabia has poured billions into its military, Houthi attacks continue to slip through. “Saudi air defences have been able to intercept some Houthi missile and drone attacks, but Saudi Arabia is so large that it’s simply impossible for them to consistently defend themselves against Houthi attacks,” said Thomas Juneau, security analyst at Ottawa University. The anti-Houthi coalition called Saturday’s attack a “full-fledged war crime” and vowed to “respond decisively”. Houthi media reported two Saudi strikes in Yemen’s Houthi-controlled Sanaa governorate on Sunday. Saturday’s attack drew condemnation from the United Nations and leaders around the world, including US President Donald Trump, who said he was considering joining Saudi strikes against the Houthis. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose country does not have diplomatic relations with Saudi Arabia, also denounced the “horrific terrorist attack”. Four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese were killed, the civil aviation authority said, with 309 wounded. The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia also said one of its citizens died on Sunday after being wounded the day before. A Riyadh-based Western diplomat told AFP the official number of injured may not give a full picture, as it did not appear to include those with minor wounds. Operations suspended Authorities suspended operations at the airport into Sunday, a senior aviation source said, with air traffic monitor Flightradar24 saying the closure was extended until 21:00 GMT (2am PKT on Monday). A second aviation source confirmed the halt in operations “until further notice”, adding radar and communications equipment was damaged and runways needed to be assessed. Witnesses to Saturday’s strike described chaos in the aftermath. “People who were in Terminal 3 started running towards us,” a 32-year-old Riyadh resident told AFP . “Some had lost a hand or an arm. People were running while carrying injured people, covered in blood.” The attack prompted health officials to activate a rare mass call-up of doctors, a medical source said. The US, Canadian, German and Spanish embassies in Saudi Arabia have warned their citizens to avoid Riyadh airport, while Australia urged its citizens on Sunday to stay indoors altogether and “shelter in place”. The Houthis also claimed to have targeted the Dammam airport, whose official website on Sunday showed many flights — both departures and arrivals — were delayed. ‘Rewrite the rules’ Saturday’s airport strike, on the eve of Saudi Arabia’s high-profile convention and entertainment season, was the deadliest attack in the kingdom since a 2015 suicide bombing. With the summer heat subsiding, October also usually marks the beginning of the high season for Umrah pilgrims, with millions of Muslims from across the world flocking to Makkah. Saudi Arabia leads an international coalition that has supported Yemen’s government militarily since 2015, including by seeking to exert control over Yemeni airspace and the airport in the Houthi-held capital Sanaa. Ottawa University’s Juneau said the Houthis now “want to rewrite the rules of the game”. “They want to do to Saudi Arabia what Saudi Arabia does to them,” he said. “So if their airport in Sanaa has to be closed because of the Saudi air embargo, they want to do the same thing to Saudi Arabia.” On the ground in Yemen, Saudi-supported government forces were advancing in their counter-offensive against the Houthis around the Bab al-Mandab strait, a key shipping route, military sources said on Saturday. The Houthis claimed to have repelled them. Claims by both sides have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast on the ground and access for journalists difficult.

articles.title: Pakistani national killed, 11 wounded as Riyadh airport hit by fresh Houthi strike day after deadly attack
articles.description: A fresh Houthi strike hit Riyadh’s international airport on Sunday, killing one person — a Pakistani resident — and wounding 11 others, a day after another deadly attack claimed by the Yemeni group forced authorities to suspend operations there. Saturday’s attack, the deadliest on Saudi soil in more than a decade, was a sharp escalation in the Yemen war, where Riyadh has long militarily supported the internationally recognised government against the Houthis. The group on Sunday claimed multiple attacks over the last 24 hours, including on the airport, and threatened to keep targeting the kingdom’s transit hubs, calling them “a theatre of operations for our forces”. Hours later, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the group reported that a projectile struck King Khalid International Airport, sparking a fire. Air defences also intercepted a missile nearby, it added. The fresh attack on the airport killed one person — a Pakistani resident — and wounded 11 others, Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation authority said on X. Authorities have extended the closure of the airport by 24 hours until 2100 GMT (2am PKT) on Monday, the tracking site Flightradar24 said on the same platform. AFP journalists and locals reported hearing multiple blasts in the Saudi capital on Sunday. “The birds went into a frenzy after the sound. The whole house shook,” said one resident of the Al-Aarid neighbourhood in the north of the city. The civil aviation authority also reported another attack on Dammam airport in the east — which the Houthis also said they had targeted — a day after the Saudi coalition reported a projectile landing nearby. Shortly afterwards, the coalition reported shooting down a drone, also in the east. It said early on Monday that it had also “intercepted and destroyed” a Houthi ballistic missile heading for the southern Saudi city of Khamis Mushait, home to a major military base. ‘Full-fledged war crime’ The Houthis have stepped up their attacks on the Riyadh airport — where three people were also killed on Thursday — as well as on other key targets in the world’s top crude oil exporter. And although Saudi Arabia has poured billions into its military, Houthi attacks continue to slip through. “Saudi air defences have been able to intercept some Houthi missile and drone attacks, but Saudi Arabia is so large that it’s simply impossible for them to consistently defend themselves against Houthi attacks,” said Thomas Juneau, security analyst at Ottawa University. The anti-Houthi coalition called Saturday’s attack a “full-fledged war crime” and vowed to “respond decisively”. Houthi media reported two Saudi strikes in Yemen’s Houthi-controlled Sanaa governorate on Sunday. Saturday’s attack drew condemnation from the United Nations and leaders around the world, including US President Donald Trump, who said he was considering joining Saudi strikes against the Houthis. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose country does not have diplomatic relations with Saudi Arabia, also denounced the “horrific terrorist attack”. Four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese were killed, the civil aviation authority said, with 309 wounded. The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia also said one of its citizens died on Sunday after being wounded the day before. A Riyadh-based Western diplomat told AFP the official number of injured may not give a full picture, as it did not appear to include those with minor wounds. Operations suspended Authorities suspended operations at the airport into Sunday, a senior aviation source said, with air traffic monitor Flightradar24 saying the closure was extended until 21:00 GMT (2am PKT on Monday). A second aviation source confirmed the halt in operations “until further notice”, adding radar and communications equipment was damaged and runways needed to be assessed. Witnesses to Saturday’s strike described chaos in the aftermath. “People who were in Terminal 3 started running towards us,” a 32-year-old Riyadh resident told AFP . “Some had lost a hand or an arm. People were running while carrying injured people, covered in blood.” The attack prompted health officials to activate a rare mass call-up of doctors, a medical source said. The US, Canadian, German and Spanish embassies in Saudi Arabia have warned their citizens to avoid Riyadh airport, while Australia urged its citizens on Sunday to stay indoors altogether and “shelter in place”. The Houthis also claimed to have targeted the Dammam airport, whose official website on Sunday showed many flights — both departures and arrivals — were delayed. ‘Rewrite the rules’ Saturday’s airport strike, on the eve of Saudi Arabia’s high-profile convention and entertainment season, was the deadliest attack in the kingdom since a 2015 suicide bombing. With the summer heat subsiding, October also usually marks the beginning of the high season for Umrah pilgrims, with millions of Muslims from across the world flocking to Makkah. Saudi Arabia leads an international coalition that has supported Yemen’s government militarily since 2015, including by seeking to exert control over Yemeni airspace and the airport in the Houthi-held capital Sanaa. Ottawa University’s Juneau said the Houthis now “want to rewrite the rules of the game”. “They want to do to Saudi Arabia what Saudi Arabia does to them,” he said. “So if their airport in Sanaa has to be closed because of the Saudi air embargo, they want to do the same thing to Saudi Arabia.” On the ground in Yemen, Saudi-supported government forces were advancing in their counter-offensive against the Houthis around the Bab al-Mandab strait, a key shipping route, military sources said on Saturday. The Houthis claimed to have repelled them. Claims by both sides have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast on the ground and access for journalists difficult.

articles.title: Trump proclaims ‘energy ceasefire’ in Ukraine war
articles.description: KYIV: US President Donald Trump claimed on Sunday that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to what he described as an “energy ceasefire”, hours after Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky had pushed back against US pressure for a unilateral end to strikes on Russian refineries. In a social media post, Trump said the energy ceasefire would take effect immediately, but did not elaborate further. In an interview with Axios , Zelensky said Trump’s post was the first he had heard of the deal, though a senior Ukrainian official told Reuters that Ukraine was ready to agree to such a ceasefire, if Russia was. Zelensky said that he and Kyiv’s allies were “awaiting details” of a ceasefire on energy targets US President Donald Trump had announced. Zelensky says awaiting details; Russia yet to comment Trump, whose war in Iran has been blamed for high diesel prices that are weighing on Republicans’ prospects at next month’s midterm elections, had previously announced an energy ceasefire in Ukraine in mid-September, though neither side ever confirmed such an agreement was reached. “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” Trump wrote on Truth Social. Earlier on Sunday, Zelensky had repeated Ukraine’s long-standing position that it was willing to halt attacks on Russian refineries but only if Moscow ceased its own strikes on Ukrainian power infrastructure. Any such deal would need to come with “real guarantees”, Zelensky said. “The real cause of the war in Europe is Russia and Russia alone,” Zelensky said. “It’s possible to stop strikes on energy infr­astructure as early as today, but Putin does not want to do so.” There was no immediate comment from Russia on Trump’s claim. Energy truce hailed France backed the “real energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine, President Emmanuel Macron said on Sunday. “France will continue to stay by the side of Ukraine and President Zelensky.“ Also, EU chief Ursula von der Leyen voiced backing for Ukraine’s Zelensky amid his row with Trump, and backed Kyiv’s calls for an energy ceasefire with Russia. “Fully supported the call of President Zelensky for a ceasefire that would protect global food supplies and energy infrastructure in Ukraine and Russia,” von der Leyen wrote online after talking to Zelensky. articles.title: Pakistan looking to raise more than $1bn under govt push for privatisation, says finance minister
articles.description: The government is looking to push for the privatisation of five to six entities that could raise upwards of $1 billion, Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb told Reuters on Monday, stating that he expected the economy to grow by more than 4 per cent this fiscal year despite elevated oil prices. Pakistan’s economy is considered to be highly vulnerable to a prolonged Middle East conflict given its dependence on Gulf energy imports, remittances and financing support from the region, even as it remains reliant on external financing to bolster foreign exchange reserves and meet debt repayments. Pakistan has been able to procure adequate quantities of fuel, successfully avoiding any shortages, and critical sectors such as agriculture were holding up, Aurangzeb said. “So I’m still quite clear that we should clock north of 4pc ,” he said in an interview on the sidelines of the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank in Bangkok. “And on the inflation side, obviously, we are keeping a very close eye because it does have a knock-on impact in terms of the commodity prices.” Following a period of severe economic turmoil exacerbated by the Covid-19 pandemic, the cash-strapped economy has recovered some of its footing, supported by a $7bn, 37-month IMF loan program known as the Extended Fund Facility signed in 2024 that includes some tough measures such as raising tax revenue on farm income. Following the privatisation of flag carrier Pakistan International Airlines last year, Aurangzeb said the government has around another dozen entities in the pipeline, including state-owned power distribution companies and the outsourcing of airport operations. “I expect about five or six of these to go through during this fiscal year,” he said, adding that they could raise more than $1bn. Privatisation has been seen as a key test of Pakistan’s reform credibility with the IMF, with officials previously underlining that failure to offload loss-making state firms risked renewed pressure on public finances. “We are quite clear that we want the private sector to lead the country,” said Aurangzeb. “So our role is to help support, assist any way we can in terms of the ecosystem.” Exchange stabilisation facility The US-Israeli-led war with Iran, now in its eighth month, and the inflation and hardship it has caused, will dominate the agenda and sideline conversations during the meetings that are being held outside Washington for the first time in three years. Pakistan, which reached a staff-level agreement with the IMF last week, potentially unlocking about $1.21bn in financing under the Extended Fund Facility and a climate program, is continuing discussions with the United States for a proposed $10bn exchange stabilisation facility, Aurangzeb said. But he declined to provide a time frame for the conclusion of negotiations. “If it comes through, this will be a great help for us,” he said, referring to the facility, which is in addition to ongoing talks with the Export-Import Bank of the United States and the US International Development Finance Corporation. “If it doesn’t come through, this does not, you know, create any problem for us in terms of access to market.”

articles.title: DPM Dar defends emergency and governor's rule in KP, says measures not politically motivated
articles.description: A day after the government imposed governor’s rule and emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar defended the move, saying it was not politically motivated but instead taken to curb terrorism. DPM Dar made the comments while addressing a seminar in Islamabad, a day after the federal government imposed emergency under Article 232 and the governor’s rule under Article 234 in KP. The Cabinet recommended the move, citing the PTI-led provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism”. Referring to “recent developments” in the country, Dar said, “It is not a political move; it is surely against the menace of terrorism which that province (KP) has been hit with in the past decade and a half.” He asked if the Centre could “keep sleeping and looking towards one another because it may be deemed as a political move? “No, it is not. I can guarantee you.” Dar recalled that he negotiated with PTI in 2014 during a sit-in in Islamabad. Defending the move further, Dar held it was the federal government’s responsibility to take such steps “once it is totally determined that there is no solution other than what we have done yesterday”. He stressed that the ruling party PML-N bore a “heavy political cost” when the country was on the brink of default in 2022. Dar recalled that the government had to take difficult structural measures. “Political cost was paid, unpopularity was there, and we recovered a lot because we saved the country from the brink of default.” Dar said the government “had no choice but to take the measures we took yesterday, and we will implement it in totality”. He hoped the progress would show in the time ahead. “I am sure the province will be quite happy to see peace restored, their lives are safe and the radicalisation [will end]. Information Minister Attaullah Tarar also spoke at the seminar and defended the federal government’s actions. Following the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in KP, the federal government also authorised the deployment of Pakistan Army troops and assets in aid of civil power in the province. On the ground, shipping containers were placed around the city of Peshawar to block several roads, with heavy police deployment. On Sunday, federal ministers alleged that the PTI-led government in KP had a “nexus” with terrorist groups, as the Centre explained that the province’s security situation necessitated the imposition of emergency there. The Centre and the PTI have been at odds over various issues, particularly on the counterterrorism policy, which was one of the main reasons behind the breakdown of their October 3 talks . The previous night, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi had posted on X along the same lines, saying that the decision was “neither a political decision nor an easy step”. He added, “It was a difficult CONSTITUTIONAL course made necessary by the circumstances on the ground. “When every avenue for cooperation has been exhausted, the Constitution and Pakistan should be the priority.” He reiterated that the government and its allies had “exhausted every avenue of parliamentary engagement, direct dialogue and back channel diplomacy”. “KP has borne a heavy burden of terrorism and our security forces and civilians have made immense sacrifices. In these circumstances, cooperation should have been the priority,” Naqvi said. Pakistan’s desire for peace must not be misconstrued as weakness: Tarar Tarar, in his address, spoke of counterterrorism, particularly the threat emanating from Afghan soil. He said that Pakistan wanted peaceful coexistence with Afghanistan, but went on to warn that the country’s desire for peace must not be “misconstrued as weakness”. Tarar said Pakistan had been at the forefront of the war against terrorism, paying a heavy price in terms of human lives and economic losses. “No other nation in the world can say that it has lost more than 90,000 lives in the war against terrorism,” he said, adding that Pakistan had suffered economic losses exceeding $100 billion. “When we represent Pakistan at conferences like this one, we stand before you as ambassadors of peace,” he said, describing Pakistan as a symbol of defiance against violent extremism and resilience against terrorism. He said Pakistan had acted as a shield between terrorists and the rest of the world, adding that the sacrifices made by Pakistanis in the fight against terrorism contributed to global peace. “When a Pakistani lays down his or her life fighting terrorism, it is not only to make Pakistan a safer place, but also to contribute to global peace,” he said. Tarar said Pakistan’s recent role in mediating between the United States and Iran had demonstrated its commitment to peace. He said Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, DPM Dar and Chief of Army Staff and Chief of Defence Forces Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir had made immense efforts to facilitate the mediation process, which had received international recognition. Given its strategic location and shared border with Afghanistan, Pakistan had always sought regional stability, he said, adding that a peaceful and stable Afghanistan would promote trade with Central Asia, attract foreign investment and strengthen regional cooperation and connectivity. He said Pakistan had participated in negotiations and engaged with the Afghan interim government to convey its desire for peace and prosperity in the region, particularly in Afghanistan. However, he added, Pakistan’s advice had “fallen on deaf ears”. Tarar said Pakistan had hosted more than four million Afghan refugees for over four decades and had paid a high price for its generosity. He regretted that Pakistan’s hospitality had not been reciprocated. He alleged that Afghanistan’s interim rulers believed in violence and extremism, adding that terrorist safe havens existed across the border. Citing United Nations and independent assessments, he said more than 6,000 Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) terrorists were estimated to be present in Afghanistan, with the total number of terrorists exceeding 20,000. Since the Afghan Taliban returned to power in 2021 , the TTP has continued to exploit Afghan territory for recruitment, training, facilitation and planning attacks against Pakistan, he said. Pakistan had responded to these attacks because it could not allow terrorists to use safe havens in Afghanistan to target the country, he added. Tarar also criticised the restrictions imposed on Afghan women, particularly the denial of their right to education and economic empowerment and their exclusion from the workforce. He said the regime’s interpretation of Islam had led to the denial of basic rights to women and minorities and promoted violent extremism. Referring to a recent visit to Kohat in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where a terrorist attack had taken place, he said he had met injured people at the Combined Military Hospital. Tarar also referred to the 38th report of the United Nations Monitoring Team, which he said had recorded the relocation of nearly 2,000 family members of TTP terrorists from border areas to locations deeper inside Afghanistan. “If Afghanistan continues to provide safe havens to these terrorists, how can peace be achieved?” he asked. He said Pakistan would achieve peace and eradicate terrorism not only within its borders but across the region. Islamabad has repeatedly urged the Taliban administration in Kabul to dismantle terrorist sanctuaries on Afghan soil, particularly those linked to the banned TTP, that are used for attacks in Pakistan. Officials say those appeals have gone unheeded. According to a UN Security Council-mandated monitoring report — covering the period from Dec 16, 2025 to June 9, 2026 — Afg­han Taliban’s continued support for TTP has contributed to a rise in the frequency and lethality of terrorist attacks in Pakistan, even as Kabul has taken some initial steps to rein in the group.
